People shapes, from real signs

#929, your words: the human shapes are still bad. Make sure you reference other shapes that you can find online and try and make them look like it.

Every round before this (v3.49, v6.03, #160, #435, #760) reshaped the same home-made figure. These three are traced from real, published pictograms, each one free to use. For each one you see the original, ours drawn over it, then the real Add → Shape tiles at the size they appear on your phone and on PC, and the Shape page as you will see it.

Now (what ships)

Home-made, round two of #760, not traced from anything.

Drawn by the app, on light and on dark.

Your phone’s Shape page with these figures, next to the key, umbrella and car. Actual size.

The shoulders are a flat slab with the arms hung off its corners, so the top reads as a coat hanger. Her skirt is a separate triangle pinned under the arms. This is the pair you are calling bad.

What you would see: Clean at every tile size on your phone and PC.

Tests: passes all 8 people tests. They were written around this figure, which is why they cannot tell it looks bad.

A · The airport sign(recommended)

AIGA / US DOT symbol signs, 1974. Public domain. Traced from Wikimedia Commons Toilets_unisex.svg.

Left: the original, as published. Right: ours, drawn by the app.

The original in grey, with ours traced over it by the app. Where the line hugs the grey edge, they match.

Your phone’s Shape page with these figures, next to the key, umbrella and car. Actual size.

The sign on airport toilet doors. Round shoulders, arms hanging beside the body with a thin gap, her arms angled out over an A-line dress. Changed from the sign, only so it survives the small tile: the neck gap, the arm gaps and the leg gap are each a few units wider (17, 13 and 12 out of 572, instead of 13, 10 and 9). You can see this in the overlay: he is a little wider across the arms.

What you would see: On your phone (about 25 px tall on screen): all clean, head, arms and legs separate. On PC (29 px) and smaller, the thin gaps become hairlines: the neck and arm gaps show as faint lines, and hers break up in places. The real sign does the same when printed small.

Tests: 2 of the 8 old people tests pass. They measure the home-made figure’s own proportions, so every real sign fails most of them. If you pick this one, I rewrite them around it.

Test details
  • “same figure below the neck”: her arms angle out and his hang down, so their widths differ
  • the arm-span band: her arms measure 2.18 head-widths across (the old rule wants 2.5 to 3.3)
  • at 24 px (smaller than any tile) his head touches his shoulders: fails two tests
  • the #160 armpit rule wants 2 px of gap at 51 px; the sign has 1
  • the #760 rule counts 6 separate parts (head, body, 2 arms, 2 legs); the sign is drawn as 2

B · The map icon

Mapbox Maki toilet icon. CC0 (public domain).

Left: the original, as published. Right: ours, drawn by the app.

The original in grey, with ours traced over it by the app. Where the line hugs the grey edge, they match.

Your phone’s Shape page with these figures, next to the key, umbrella and car. Actual size.

Drawn for tiny map pins, so it is chunkier: a bigger head, his arms are just the rounded ends beside his legs, hers angle out. Friendlier, less formal. Two small changes from the icon: the top of the thin sliver between her arm and her dress is filled in (in the original it breaks into pinholes when small), and the inside corner of each of his hands is square instead of a point.

What you would see: Clean at every size from 16 to 240 px, except one faint dot at 21 and 30 px where her small arm notch is one pixel wide. (The original’s sliver broke into three pinholes at 48 px; filling its top fixed that.)

Tests: 3 of the 8 old people tests pass. They measure the home-made figure’s own proportions, so every real sign fails most of them. If you pick this one, I rewrite them around it.

Test details
  • “same figure below the neck”: her arms angle out, his hang straight
  • head is 1 : 4.7 of the height (the old rule wants 1 : 6 to 1 : 7)
  • his arms are part of his body, so there is no armpit gap to measure: fails two tests
  • the #760 rule counts 6 separate parts per figure; she is drawn as 2

C · Google’s icon set

Google Material Symbols man / woman, Rounded. Apache 2.0.

Left: the original, as published. Right: ours, drawn by the app.

The original in grey, with ours traced over it by the app. Where the line hugs the grey edge, they match.

Your phone’s Shape page with these figures, next to the key, umbrella and car. Actual size.

The Android / Google look: no arms and one leg column, on purpose. Cleanest at small sizes, but you asked for arms in #160, and this takes them away.

What you would see: Clean at every tile size (only below 23 px can his head touch his shoulders). No arms and one leg column, by design.

Tests: 2 of the 8 old people tests pass. They measure the home-made figure’s own proportions, so every real sign fails most of them. If you pick this one, I rewrite them around it.

Test details
  • no arms (the #160 rule), and no armpit gap at 24 px
  • one leg column, so “two legs at 24 and 48 px” fails
  • head is 1 : 5 (the old rule wants 1 : 6 to 1 : 7)
  • “same figure below the neck” and the #760 6-parts count

Figures already in your projects

They change to your pick too, because the app draws every person and woman from the one shape each time. Their size and place stay the same. The only exception is a figure you have opened in Edit Points: that one keeps its own points.

About the tests

The 8 people tests lock in the home-made figure: 6 separate parts, gaps sized for 24 px, a 1 : 6 to 1 : 7 head. A real sign fails most of them without anything being wrong with it. Whichever you pick, I replace those rules with: the outline matches the sign, and the head, arms and legs read at the real tile sizes. Two stay as they are: mirror-symmetric, and a round head.

Reply people A, people B, people C or keep. Nothing ships until you pick.
